summary:
Base Commander: Moon and Mars is an educational 3D game in which the student runs a base on the Moon or Mars and must keep it alive until the end of the mission. It runs in the browser with no installation, in Ukrainian and English.

What we built. An engineering simulator with six life-support systems (energy, air, water, food, radiation, equipment wear), four modes, three difficulty levels, 29 events, and a built-in Spacepedia of 14 articles. All actions are carried out by astronauts, so there are no "magic" buttons.

What problem it solves. School knowledge of physics, chemistry, and engineering often stays abstract. In the game, the student sees how resources are linked in chains and that every failure has a cause. The report with a cause tree explains mistakes, and "IF… THEN…" rules introduce programming.

Why it matters. The game builds systems and engineering thinking and interest in STEM in an accessible format.
details:
What the project does and how it works. Base Commander: Moon and Mars is an educational 3D browser game, with no installation required, available in Ukrainian and English. The student runs a base on the Moon or Mars and must keep it alive until the end of the mission. They select an astronaut, give an order with a tap, and monitor six systems: energy, air, water, food, radiation, and equipment wear. All actions are carried out by astronauts, they take a certain amount of time, and they can fail. The base is affected by 29 events and crises, and resources are linked in chains: ice goes to the melter, then to the water tank, then to electrolysis, and oxygen is produced. After the mission, the player receives a report with a score, charts, and a cause tree of failures.

Advantages. The game works on any device with a browser and has touch controls. It has three difficulty levels, a sandbox with a custom seed, and a teacher mode in which the built-in encyclopedia, the Spacepedia, is fully unlocked. The numbers in the game are educational approximations of real values. For example, a person needs about 0.84 kg of oxygen per day, and the regenerator returns 90% of water. Every event explains why it happened and what NASA engineers would do.

Expected impact. The game makes school physics, chemistry, and engineering tangible, develops systems thinking, and introduces students to programming through the automation rules "IF… THEN…". It raises interest in STEM and space, and also connects the space theme with Ukraine: Drohobych salt and Donetsk coal become part of the mission.

Tools and technologies. JavaScript and WebGL were used, along with the Three.js library. The game is hosted at https://fable53.dmtc.org.ua/.

Creativity. Instead of "magic" buttons, the game simulates the physical actions of the crew and cause-and-effect chains. The Spacepedia unlocks at the moment a student encounters a phenomenon. The automation rules become a first step toward programming, and Ukrainian symbols, namely salt, coal, and Drohobych sausage, are combined with real ISS technologies. The Gate Review scoring principle imitates NASA's approach.

Factors our team considered. We considered realism: the game uses educational approximations of real data. We considered accessibility: the game works without installation, has two languages, and supports touch controls. We took into account the age and preparation of players: "Young Astronaut" has hints and 50% more supplies, while "Expert" offers a real challenge. We considered pedagogy: the game explains the causes of mistakes rather than only showing the result. Safety carries the greatest weight in scoring, at 35%, because the main goal is to bring the crew back alive. Finally, we considered an international perspective: the map in the menu shows the borders of Ukraine under international law.
